pos: adj. (that cannot be put out; of the fire prepared for the impenitent)
etymology: From un- and quench, rendering the Greek asbestos — not extinguishable. The same root gives the mineral name; the point of the word is not heat but permanence.
biblical_def: John the Baptist preached it before Christ preached it: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12; and again Luke 3:17). The figure is a threshing floor at the end of harvest, where the winnowing fan separates what is kept from what is burned, and the separation is final. Our Lord uses the same term without softening it: better to enter into life maimed “than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched” (Mark 9:43). The Old Testament supplies the image He is drawing on, and it is the last verse of Isaiah: “their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched” (Isaiah 66:24). Two things are asserted together in that line — the worm does not die and the fire is not put out — and both halves say the same thing about duration. The adjective is therefore doing precise doctrinal work. It does not describe how hot the fire is; it forecloses the hope that it will one day burn itself out, and with it forecloses annihilationism and universalism alike.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unquenchable as that cannot be quenched or extinguished, and applies it to fire and to thirst.
webster_full: UNQUENCHABLE, a. That cannot be quenched or extinguished; inextinguishable; as unquenchable fire or flame.
2. That cannot be repressed or allayed; as unquenchable thirst.
QUENCH, v.t. To extinguish; to put out; as, to quench flame.
2. To still; to quiet; to repress; as, to quench a passion or emotion.
FAN, n. An instrument used for winnowing grain, by throwing it up and blowing away the chaff.
scriptures: Matthew 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Luke 3:17
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and will gather the wheat into his garner; but the chaff he will burn with fire unquenchable.
Mark 9:43
And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched:
Isaiah 66:24

And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.
corruption_summary: The one adjective that forbids an end to the fire is explained away by the two doctrines that require one.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism, sometimes called conditional immortality, argues that the fire is unquenchable only in the sense that nothing can interrupt it until it has consumed its fuel, after which the wicked cease to exist. The argument requires the word to mean the opposite of what it says. An unquenchable fire is one that cannot be put out; a fire that goes out when the fuel is gone has simply been quenched by exhaustion. Isaiah 66:24 blocks the reading twice over by pairing the fire with a worm that does not die — if the objects of judgment were consumed, the worm would starve. Evangelicals who have adopted this position in recent decades have not found a new exegesis; they have found the doctrine intolerable and adjusted the vocabulary.

Universalism takes the other road and makes the fire remedial — a purifying furnace from which all eventually emerge. This is Origen's error, condemned in the early church and revived in our own time under the euphemism of the larger hope. Neither Testament offers it. The fan separates wheat from chaff and the two go to different places; the chaff is not refined into wheat. The Confession states the biblical doctrine without flinching: the wicked shall be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction. It is not a doctrine any faithful man preaches with pleasure, and the Saviour who taught it more plainly than anyone else in Scripture wept over the city that would not come to Him.
roots_summary: Greek asbestos (G762), unquenchable — Matthew 3:12, Mark 9:43, Luke 3:17; Hebrew kabah, to be quenched — Isaiah 66:24.
roots_lines: Greek asbestos (G762) — not extinguishable; Matthew 3:12, Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Luke 3:17.
Greek ptuon (G4425) — the winnowing fan; Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17, its only occurrences.
Greek achuron (G892) — chaff; what the fan separates and the fire consumes.
Hebrew kabah — to be quenched or extinguished; Isaiah 66:24, negated, and Isaiah 42:3 of the smoking flax He will not quench.
Mark 9:48 repeats Isaiah 66:24 verbatim as the Lord's own commentary on the word.
usage: “He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” — the winnowing fan and a final separation.
“Their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched” — both halves say duration.
The word forbids the two escapes: it does not burn out, and it does not purify.

pos: n. (a transliterated Hebrew plural, hosts or armies; in the title Lord of Sabaoth, the LORD of hosts)
etymology: Hebrew tsebaoth, the plural of tsaba, an army or host, carried untranslated into the Greek of the New Testament and thence into the Authorized Version. It has nothing to do with sabbath, which is a different word entirely.
biblical_def: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both times in the divine title. Paul quotes Isaiah: “Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha” (Romans 9:29) — the prophet's original reading “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isaiah 1:9). The title is the guarantee of the remnant. James uses it for something else and the choice is deliberate: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (James 5:4). He is addressing rich men who have defrauded their workers, and he tells them whose ears have received the complaint — not a distant deity but the Commander of armies. The hosts are the angelic armies, the stars in their courses, and the armies of Israel; the title gathers all created power under one Sovereign. Where Scripture wants to say that God is able to do what He has promised, and that no wrong escapes His notice, this is the name it reaches for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Sabaoth as armies or hosts, retained in the title Lord of Sabaoth, and distinguishes it from Sabbath.
webster_full: SABAOTH, n. Armies; hosts; a Hebrew word retained in the phrase Lord of Sabaoth, that is, Lord of hosts.
HOST, n. An army; a number of men embodied for war.
2. Any great number or multitude.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
SABBATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor.
scriptures: Romans 9:29
And as Esaias said before, Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha.
James 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
Isaiah 1:9
Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.
James 5:1
Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.
corruption_summary: The title is confused with Sabbath, and the God of armies is refashioned into a deity with no armies at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, beyond the persistent confusion with Sabbath that even hymn-singers make. The principle to recover is what the title asserts. A God of hosts is a God who commands, who musters, and who acts — and modern religious speech has been steadily emptied of exactly that. The deity of much contemporary devotion is affectionate and unarmed, present to comfort and unable to intervene, and hymns that once named the LORD of hosts as a bulwark now sit oddly in congregations that no longer mean it. Luther knew what he was writing when he put Lord Sabaoth his name into the second stanza and told the singers that the outcome of the battle was already settled.

James 5:4 shows the practical edge of the title and it cuts against a common failure of application. The defrauded labourer has no recourse against a wealthy employer; the wages are withheld and there is no court he can afford. James does not tell him to organise, and he does not tell him to accept it. He tells the rich man that the cry has already reached the ears of the Commander of armies. The doctrine of God's sovereignty is not a sedative for the oppressed but a warning to the oppressor, and the churches have often preached it backwards — urging patience on the defrauded while leaving the defrauder undisturbed.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaba, army or host, plural tsebaoth — over 280 times as LORD of hosts; transliterated as Greek sabaoth (G4519) in Romans 9:29, James 5:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsebaoth — hosts, armies; the plural behind the title LORD of hosts, most frequent in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.
Greek sabaoth (G4519) — a transliteration, not a translation; Romans 9:29 and James 5:4, its only New Testament occurrences.
Hebrew tsaba — an army, and also the appointed service of a soldier; Job 7:1 uses it of man's appointed time on earth.
1 Samuel 17:45 gives the title its clearest setting: David comes to Goliath in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel.
Isaiah 1:9, quoted at Romans 9:29, ties the title to the doctrine of the remnant — the hosts preserve a seed.
usage: “Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed” — the armies of heaven preserve a remnant.
“Entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” — the defrauded labourer has a Commander for an advocate.
Sabaoth is hosts, and has nothing to do with sabbath.

pos: n. (Aramaic, thou hast forsaken me; the fourth word from the cross)
etymology: Aramaic shebaqtani, from shebaq, to leave or forsake — preserved untranslated by both Matthew and Mark, who then give the sense in Greek. The retention of the sound is itself a kind of testimony: the evangelists kept the syllables the bystanders actually heard.
biblical_def: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Mark preserves the same cry with the Aramaic form of the divine name: “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani” (Mark 15:34). The words are the opening line of Psalm 22 — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?” (Psalm 22:1) — a psalm that goes on to describe pierced hands and feet, garments parted, and lots cast for vesture, a thousand years before the event. To quote its first line from the cross is to claim the whole psalm. What was forsaken was not the union of the Person; the Son did not cease to be the Son, and the Trinity was not divided. What He bore was the judicial abandonment due to the sin imputed to Him: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The cry is the sound of penal substitution. And Psalm 22 does not end in the dark — it ends with the ends of the world remembering and turning unto the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this Aramaic word; it is preserved untranslated in Matthew and Mark, who supply the sense in the same verse.
webster_full: SABACHTHANI — Aramaic, retained untranslated in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34, and rendered in the same verses: why hast thou forsaken me.
FORSAKE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from.
2. To abandon; to renounce; to reject.
3. In scripture, God forsakes his people, when he withdraws his aid, or the light of his countenance.
ABANDON, v.t. To forsake entirely; as to abandon a hopeless enterprise.
scriptures: Matthew 27:46
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Mark 15:34
And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Psalm 22:1
My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
2 Corinthians 5:21
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
corruption_summary: The cry is used either to divide the Trinity or to deny that any real forsaking took place, and Scripture permits neither.
corruption_paragraphs: One error preaches the cross as though the Father turned on the Son in hatred, or as though the Godhead were for three hours torn apart. Some popular hymnody has come close to saying it. The divine nature cannot be divided and the Persons cannot be separated; the Son remained the beloved Son throughout, and it is the same Gospel that records Him commending His spirit into His Father's hands a little later. What He endured was the withdrawal of the comfortable sense of the Father's favour and the bearing of the curse due to imputed sin — real, and terrible, and not a rupture in the Trinity.

The opposite error empties the cry of its content by making it merely a recitation, as though the Lord were only citing a psalm to point the bystanders to a prophecy. He was indeed claiming Psalm 22, but the anguish was His own and the abandonment was real. Liberal treatments go further and read the line as the collapse of a disappointed man, which requires ignoring both the psalm's triumphant ending and the deliberate My God — a cry of faith, not of unbelief. The Reformed doctrine holds what both errors drop: a true forsaking, judicially borne, by a Person who never for an instant ceased to be the Son of God.
roots_summary: Aramaic shebaqtani (G4518), thou hast forsaken me — Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34; Hebrew azab in Psalm 22:1; Greek egkataleipo (G1459) in the evangelists' translation.
roots_lines: Aramaic sabachthani (G4518) — thou hast forsaken me; Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 only.
Aramaic lama (G2982) — why; kept with the verb in both accounts.
Hebrew azab — to leave, forsake; Psalm 22:1, the line the Lord quoted.
Greek egkataleipo (G1459) — to leave behind, abandon; the evangelists' rendering, and the very verb negated in Hebrews 13:5 for the believer.
Hebrews 13:5 is the counterpart promise: I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee — because He was forsaken.
usage: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” — the fourth word, and the darkest.
To quote the first line of Psalm 22 is to claim the whole psalm.
He was forsaken so that His people never will be.

pos: n. (a great sea creature; the Authorized Version's rendering for the largest inhabitants of the deep)
etymology: Old English hwael, a large sea-beast. The Authorized Version uses it for Hebrew tannin (a great sea creature or monster) and for Greek ketos (a huge fish or sea-beast) — in neither case a term of modern zoological classification.
biblical_def: The word enters Scripture on the fifth day: “And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind” (Genesis 1:21). It is the first appearance of the verb create since verse one, which is a mark of how the text regards these creatures — not as chaos-monsters wrestled into submission, as the surrounding nations told it, but as made, and pronounced good. Job asks, “Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?” (Job 7:12), and Ezekiel uses the figure for Pharaoh thrashing in his rivers (Ezekiel 32:2). But the weight of the word rests on our Lord's use of it: “For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). Jonah records that “the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah” (Jonah 1:17). Christ takes that history as history and makes it the one sign granted to a generation demanding proof — the sign of the prophet Jonas, which is burial and resurrection.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the whale as the largest of marine animals, of the order Cete, and notes the scriptural use for great fishes of the sea.
webster_full: WHALE, n. The general name of an order of animals inhabiting the ocean, arranged in zoology under the name of Cete or Cetacea.
2. In scripture, a name given to great fishes or sea-monsters generally.
MONSTER, n. An animal of a form different from that which nature usually produces.
DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.
SIGN, n. That by which anything is shown, made known or represented; a token; a wonder.
scriptures: Matthew 12:40
For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
Genesis 1:21
And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good.
Jonah 1:17
Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
Job 7:12
Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?
corruption_summary: The great fish is made the test case for treating Old Testament narrative as legend, and the Lord who cited it as history is quietly overruled.
corruption_paragraphs: Jonah has long been the standard exhibit for the claim that the historical books contain legendary material — a moral fable about a reluctant prophet, not a record of events. The difficulty for that reading is not zoological but doctrinal. Christ founded an argument about His own burial and resurrection on the case, offered it as the only sign His generation would receive, and in the following verse spoke of the men of Nineveh rising in the judgment because they repented at Jonah's preaching. A sign drawn from a story that did not happen is no sign, and men who did not exist do not rise in the judgment. To make Jonah a fable is to correct the Lord Jesus on a matter of fact He treated as decisive.

A second and lesser confusion arises from pressing the English word into modern taxonomy and then declaring an error, since ketos and Hebrew tannin denote a great sea-creature without specifying an order of mammals. The Authorized Version is not making a claim about cetaceans. Jonah 1:17 says the LORD prepared a great fish, which locates the event where the text locates it — in the providence of God, not in the ordinary habits of marine life. The miracle was never that a fish was large. It was that God appointed it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tannin, a great sea creature — Genesis 1:21, Ezekiel 32:2, Job 7:12; Greek ketos (G2785), a sea-monster — Matthew 12:40, its only occurrence.
roots_lines: Hebrew tannin — sea creature, monster, serpent; Genesis 1:21 where God creates them, and Ezekiel 32:2 of Pharaoh.
Greek ketos (G2785) — a huge fish or sea-beast; Matthew 12:40 only.
Hebrew dag gadol — a great fish; Jonah 1:17, prepared by the LORD.
Genesis 1:21 uses bara, to create, for the first time since Genesis 1:1 — these creatures are made, not subdued.
Matthew 12:39-41 makes the episode the sign of the prophet Jonas and appeals to the Ninevites as real men who repented.
usage: “Three days and three nights in the whale's belly” — the one sign given to an evil generation.
“God created great whales” — made and called good, not chaos to be conquered.
The LORD prepared the fish; the appointing is the miracle.

pos: n. and adj. (unsteadiness, vacillation; the divided mind that Scripture forbids in prayer and in profession)
etymology: From waver, to move to and fro, of the same family as wave. It renders two Greek words: diakrino in James, to be divided in judgment with oneself, and aklines in Hebrews, literally not-leaning.
biblical_def: “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)” (Hebrews 10:23). The parenthesis carries the argument: steadfastness is commanded not because the believer is strong but because the Promiser is faithful. The exhortation stands in a chain — let us draw near, let us hold fast, let us consider one another — and it follows immediately on the invitation to come with a true heart in full assurance (Hebrews 10:22). James applies the same principle to prayer: “But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6). The figure is exact. A wave has no direction of its own; it goes wherever the last gust pushed it. And the consequence is stated without softening: “For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord” (James 1:7). Wavering is not the same as weakness of faith — the father who cried “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief” was heard. It is a divided will, asking God for what it is not resolved to receive from Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wavering as fluctuating, being unsettled in opinion, moving to and fro like a wave.
webster_full: WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to move one way and the other.
2. To fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion; to vacillate; to be undetermined.
WAVERING, ppr. Fluctuating; being in doubt; undetermined.
STEDFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; constant; not fickle or wavering.
DOUBLE-MINDED, a. Having different minds at different times; unsettled; wavering.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:23
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
James 1:6
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.
James 1:7
For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord.
Hebrews 10:22
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: James 1:6 is turned into a rule that any doubt disqualifies the petitioner, which torments the weak and misses the divided heart the text names.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teachers have made this verse into a mechanism: ask without a flicker of uncertainty and the thing is granted, and if it is not granted the fault lies in the asking. Two errors are packed into that. The first mistakes wavering for the ordinary weakness of a believing heart, which Scripture everywhere treats tenderly — the man of Mark 9 was answered, Gideon was given his fleece, and Thomas was invited to put his hand into the side of the risen Christ. The second treats faith as a force that operates on God rather than a trust that rests in Him. James defines his own term two verses later: the waverer is a double minded man, unstable in all his ways — not a Christian who trembles, but a man asking God for something while keeping his options open elsewhere.

Hebrews 10:23 is corrupted from the other direction wherever perseverance is preached as sheer willpower. The verse commands holding fast and then immediately supplies the reason, and the reason is not in the holder: for he is faithful that promised. The believer's grip on Christ is real and is commanded, and it is never the ground of his security. Any exhortation to steadfastness that leaves the congregation looking at its own resolve rather than at the faithfulness of the Promiser has quoted half a verse and dropped the half that makes obedience possible.
roots_summary: Greek diakrino (G1252), to be divided in oneself — James 1:6; aklines (G186), unbending, not leaning — Hebrews 10:23, its only occurrence.
roots_lines: Greek aklines (G186) — without leaning, unwavering; Hebrews 10:23 only.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to judge between, hence to waver or dispute with oneself; James 1:6, Romans 4:20 of Abraham who staggered not.
Greek dipsuchos (G1374) — double-minded, two-souled; James 1:8 and 4:8, James's own definition of the waverer.
Greek kludon (G2830) — a surge or billow; James 1:6, the wave driven with the wind.
Romans 4:20 gives the opposite portrait: Abraham staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strong in faith.
usage: “Hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” — and the reason follows in a parenthesis.
“Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering” — a divided will, not a trembling heart.
A wave goes wherever the last gust sent it.

pos: adj. (that cannot be shifted from its place; of a ship aground, and of the saints in the work of the Lord)
etymology: From un- and moveable, rendering Greek ametakinetos — not to be moved away from a position. The Authorized Version keeps the older spelling with the medial e.
biblical_def: The word appears twice, and the two settings interpret each other. Luke uses it of Paul's ship on the sandbar off Malta: “the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves” (Acts 27:41). That is the physical picture — something so fixed that the sea itself cannot shift it, while everything around it is torn apart. Paul then takes the word for the closing charge of the great resurrection chapter: “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58). The therefore is doing the work. Fifteen chapters have argued that Christ is risen, that the dead in Christ shall rise, that this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and that death is swallowed up in victory — and the practical conclusion drawn from all of it is: stay where you are put, and keep working. The resurrection is not offered as a consolation to be felt but as a foundation to stand on. Because the grave will not hold, the labour is not wasted, and the labourer need not be moved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines immovable as that cannot be moved from its place, and figuratively as steadfast, not to be shaken in purpose.
webster_full: IMMOVABLE, a. That cannot be moved from its place; as an immovable foundation.
2. Not to be moved from a purpose; steadfast; fixed; that cannot be induced to change or alter.
3. Not to be shaken or agitated; unfeeling.
STEDFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; constant; resolute.
ABOUND, v.i. To have or possess in great quantity; to be copiously supplied.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 15:58
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Acts 27:41
And falling into a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground; and the forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable, but the hinder part was broken with the violence of the waves.
1 Corinthians 15:57
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 12:28
Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
corruption_summary: Immovability is read as temperament rather than doctrine, and the resurrection is separated from the day's work it was given to steady.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the connection Paul draws and the modern church routinely severs: the resurrection of the body is the reason for ordinary faithfulness in ordinary labour. Where the doctrine is preached at all it is usually preached at funerals, as comfort about the future, and 1 Corinthians 15:58 puts it to a different use entirely — it is the ground of steadfastness on a Tuesday. Take the resurrection away and Paul's own conclusion earlier in the chapter follows: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Every argument for pouring out a life in unnoticed service depends on an empty tomb.

A second misuse turns unmoveableness into a disposition rather than a stance — the immovable man as the one who never reconsiders anything. Webster's third sense catches the danger: not to be shaken or agitated; unfeeling. That is not the apostolic command. Paul was moved to tears, moved with compassion, and changed his travelling plans more than once; what did not move was his position in the work he had been given. The unmoveable saint is fixed where God has set him, and the ship at Malta shows the difference — the forepart held because it was aground on something solid, not because it was insensible to the sea.
roots_summary: Greek ametakinetos (G277), unmoveable — 1 Corinthians 15:58; asaleutos (G761), unshaken — Acts 27:41, Hebrews 12:28.
roots_lines: Greek ametakinetos (G277) — not to be moved away; 1 Corinthians 15:58, its only occurrence.
Greek asaleutos (G761) — unshaken, immovable; Acts 27:41 of the grounded ship and Hebrews 12:28 of the kingdom.
Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled, stedfast; joined to it in 1 Corinthians 15:58.
Greek kenos (G2756) — empty, vain; 1 Corinthians 15:58, the labour that is not in vain.
Hebrews 12:28 supplies the reason a saint may be unmoveable: he is receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved.
usage: “Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” — the conclusion of the resurrection chapter.
“The forepart stuck fast, and remained unmoveable” — fixed because it was aground on something solid.
Your labour is not in vain, because the grave could not hold Him.

pos: n. pl. (menaces; the declared intention to do harm, whether by persecutors of the church or by masters over servants)
etymology: From Old English threatian, to press or urge, hence to menace. The Greek apeile is a threat; the verb apeileo is used of what Christ did not do when He suffered.
biblical_def: When the Sanhedrin had commanded Peter and John not to speak at all in the name of Jesus, the church met and prayed. They did not pray for the threats to stop. “And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word” (Acts 4:29). The petition asks God to look at the threat and to change the preachers rather than the circumstances, and the answer came at once: “the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31). Saul is later found “breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts 9:1) — and was stopped on the road by the One he was threatening. The other use turns the word toward the household: “And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him” (Ephesians 6:9). Authority is real and is not to be governed by menace, because the man with authority has a Master of his own who does not respect persons.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a threatening as a menace, a declaration of an intention to punish or hurt.
webster_full: THREATENING, n. A menace; denunciation of injury; declaration of an intention to punish or to inflict evil.
THREATEN, v.t. To declare the purpose of inflicting punishment or other evil on another.
2. To menace; to terrify or attempt to terrify by menaces.
BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; liberty of speech.
RESPECT OF PERSONS, partiality; the treating of one person with more favor than another on account of rank or condition, without regard to merit.
scriptures: Acts 4:29
And now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word,
Acts 4:31
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
Acts 9:1
And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
Ephesians 6:9
And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.
corruption_summary: The church's prayer under threat is reversed — asking for the removal of opposition rather than for boldness in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:29 is one of the most quietly convicting verses in the New Testament, because it shows a congregation praying the opposite of what congregations usually pray. Under real threat of imprisonment they asked for boldness to keep speaking, not for the threat to be lifted. Much modern intercession for persecuted believers inverts this — it asks almost exclusively for relief, comfort and protection, which are proper requests, while rarely asking what the apostolic church asked for first. The saints in Acts assumed the opposition would continue and asked to be made equal to it.

Ephesians 6:9 is the neglected half of a passage usually quoted only at servants. Masters are told to do the same things — to render the same goodwill they expect — and specifically to forbear threatening, the standard instrument of ancient household authority. The reason given is theological and levelling: their Master is in heaven, and there is no respect of persons with Him. Complementarian and household order is genuinely taught in this passage, and the same passage forbids ruling by menace. Any authority in home, church or workplace that maintains itself by intimidation has abandoned the pattern Scripture actually prescribes, whatever headship language it uses to defend itself.
roots_summary: Greek apeile (G547), a threat — Acts 4:29, 9:1, Ephesians 6:9; the verb apeileo (G546) — Acts 4:17, 1 Peter 2:23.
roots_lines: Greek apeile (G547) — a threatening; Acts 4:29, Acts 9:1, Ephesians 6:9.
Greek apeileo (G546) — to threaten; Acts 4:17, and 1 Peter 2:23 where Christ suffered and threatened not.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; Acts 4:29, 4:31, what the church asked for instead of relief.
Greek prosopolepsia (G4382) — respect of persons; Ephesians 6:9, denied of the heavenly Master.
1 Peter 2:23 gives the pattern: when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.
usage: “Behold their threatenings… grant unto thy servants… boldness” — the prayer asks God to change the preachers.
“Forbearing threatening” — authority is real and does not rule by menace.
When He suffered, He threatened not.

pos: n. (a person set up to be stared at; an object of public spectacle and contempt)
etymology: A compound of gazing and stock in the old sense of a stump or post — a thing set up for people to look at. It renders Greek theatrizo, to make a theatre-show of, and a Hebrew term for public disgrace in Nahum.
biblical_def: Nahum uses the word for the sentence on Nineveh: “And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock” (Nahum 3:6). Public shaming is there a judgment of God on a cruel city. The writer to the Hebrews then applies the same idea to the church, and reverses its meaning: “Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used” (Hebrews 10:33). He is calling them to remember the former days “in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions” (Hebrews 10:32) — and the memory is offered as an encouragement, not an embarrassment. Paul uses the same figure of the apostles: “we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” (1 Corinthians 4:9). The believer is therefore warned that a measure of public contempt belongs to the calling, and the two halves of Hebrews 10:33 divide the whole church between them — some are the spectacle, and the rest are those who stood publicly with them, which in a season of reproach is the costlier half.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gazing-stock as a person gazed at with scorn or abhorrence, an object of curiosity or contempt.
webster_full: GAZING-STOCK, n. A person gazed at with scorn or abhorrence; an object of curiosity or contempt.
GAZE, v.i. To fix the eyes and look steadily and earnestly; to look with eagerness or curiosity, as in admiration, astonishment, or with study.
SPECTACLE, n. A show; a gazing stock; something exhibited to view.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; contumelious or opprobrious language.
COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:33
Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used.
Hebrews 10:32
But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions;
1 Corinthians 4:9
For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
Nahum 3:6
And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock.
corruption_summary: Public shaming is now an instrument the church is tempted to wield rather than a reproach it is called to bear.
corruption_paragraphs: The gazingstock is a technology, and our age has industrialised it. What once required a magistrate and a marketplace now takes a phone, and the crowd is unlimited. Believers are on both ends of it. Where the church is despised, Hebrews 10 is exactly the passage for the moment; the reproach is expected, and the memory of having endured it is a comfort rather than a grievance. But where believers themselves have taken up the instrument — circulating an accusation, joining a pile-on, making a spectacle of an offender for an audience — they have adopted a method Scripture assigns to the judgment of Nineveh and to the enemies of the apostles. The rule of Matthew 18 is a private word first, and the crowd last, and it was written against precisely this appetite.

The second half of Hebrews 10:33 is the harder application and the one usually skipped. The congregation is commended not only for being made a spectacle but for becoming companions of them that were so used — standing publicly beside people already under reproach, and taking the reproach onto themselves. That is a costlier obedience than enduring one's own shame, because it is voluntary. It is also the plain duty of a church when one of its members, or a faithful minister elsewhere, is being made a gazingstock for the truth's sake.
roots_summary: Greek theatrizo (G2301), to make a public show of — Hebrews 10:33, its only occurrence; theatron (G2302), a spectacle — 1 Corinthians 4:9.
roots_lines: Greek theatrizo (G2301) — to expose as in a theatre; Hebrews 10:33, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek theatron (G2302) — a theatre, hence a spectacle; 1 Corinthians 4:9, and the literal building at Acts 19:29.
Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; Hebrews 10:33, and Hebrews 11:26 of the reproach of Christ that Moses esteemed greater riches.
Greek koinonos (G2844) — a partner, companion; Hebrews 10:33, of those who stood with the reproached.
Nahum 3:6 shows the same treatment as a divine judgment on a cruel city — the shame is deserved there, and undeserved in Hebrews.
usage: “Ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions” — remembered as honour, not humiliation.
“Companions of them that were so used” — standing beside the reproached is the costlier half.
“A spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” — the apostolic estimate of the ministry.

pos: n. pl. (fires; used of funeral fires for kings, of the burning of lime, and of the everlasting burnings of divine judgment)
etymology: From burn, Old English beornan. The Authorized Version uses the plural for several Hebrew terms: the ceremonial fires made for a dead king, the kilns of lime, and in Isaiah 33 the fire of God's own presence.
biblical_def: Isaiah puts the great question of the word in a single verse: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isaiah 33:14). The terror is sharpened by where it falls — on sinners in Zion, hypocrites inside the covenant community, not pagans outside it. Two verses earlier the same chapter had said, “And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire” (Isaiah 33:12). And the answer to the question is not that the fire will be avoided but that a certain man may dwell with it: “He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes” (Isaiah 33:15). The everlasting burnings are the presence of God Himself, which is destruction to the impenitent and home to the righteous. The New Testament says the same thing in four words: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). The word also has an ordinary use — the honourable funeral fires promised to Zedekiah, “with the burnings of thy fathers” (Jeremiah 34:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines burning as the act of consuming by fire, and a burning as a fire or conflagration.
webster_full: BURNING, n. The act of expelling or consuming by fire; combustion.
2. A fire; a conflagration.
3. A burning fever, or inflammation.
CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing; to destroy by burning.
LIME, n. Calcareous earth; the substance which is obtained from limestone by burning.
scriptures: Isaiah 33:14
The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?
Isaiah 33:15

He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil;
Isaiah 33:12
And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire.
Hebrews 12:29
For our God is a consuming fire.
corruption_summary: Hell is imagined as a place God sends men away to, when Isaiah locates the everlasting burnings in the presence of God Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular picture of judgment is banishment — a distant furnace where God is absent. Isaiah 33 will not support it. The question is who shall dwell with the devouring fire, and the fire in that chapter is the LORD in Zion. The same presence that is the everlasting burnings to the hypocrite is the dwelling place of the man who walks righteously. This is why the doctrine cannot be softened by making hell mere absence: it is the unshielded presence of a holy God to those who have no Mediator. Hebrews 12 makes exactly this argument and draws exactly this conclusion — let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear, for our God is a consuming fire.

The second corruption is the assumption that religious standing supplies the shielding. Isaiah's sinners are in Zion; they are inside the visible covenant people, and the fire finds them there. Verse 15 answers the question with a description of a life — honest speech, hands that refuse bribes, contempt for the gain of oppressions — which is not offered as the ground of acceptance but as the evidence of it. A congregation that assumes its membership rolls will answer Isaiah's question has misread the chapter at the precise point where it was aimed.
roots_summary: Hebrew moqed and seraphah, a burning — Isaiah 33:14, Isaiah 33:12, Jeremiah 34:5; Greek pur katanaliskon, a consuming fire — Hebrews 12:29.
roots_lines: Hebrew moqed — a hearth or burning; Isaiah 33:14, of the everlasting burnings.
Hebrew sid — lime; Isaiah 33:12, the burnings of lime, an image of total reduction.
Hebrew seraphah — a burning; Jeremiah 34:5, the honourable funeral fires of the kings.
Greek katanalisko (G2654) — to consume utterly; Hebrews 12:29, its only occurrence, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24.
Isaiah 33:15 answers Isaiah 33:14 with a life, not with an escape route.
usage: “Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” — and the answer is a man, not a hiding place.
“The sinners in Zion are afraid” — the fire finds hypocrites inside the covenant community.
“Our God is a consuming fire” — the same presence, and two destinies.

pos: n. pl. (dwellers; the Authorized Version's term in Revelation for those who dwell on the earth and are addressed with woe)
etymology: From Latin inhabitare, to dwell in. The Authorized Version uses inhabiters in Revelation where it uses inhabitants elsewhere, rendering the Greek participle katoikountes — the settled dwellers.
biblical_def: The word belongs to the Apocalypse and to its warnings. “And I beheld, and heard an angel flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice, Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth by reason of the other voices of the trumpet of the three angels, which are yet to sound!” (Revelation 8:13). And again, at the casting down of the dragon: “Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time” (Revelation 12:12). The phrase them that dwell upon the earth runs through the book as a settled description of a class — not simply everyone alive, but those whose whole portion is here, who worship the beast, whose names are not written in the book of life. Two things are said of the devil's wrath in that verse and both are comforts to the church: it is great, and it is short. He rages because he has already lost. The saints in the same chapter are described in the previous verse: “And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Revelation 12:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an inhabitant as one who dwells or resides permanently in a place, as distinguished from an occasional visitor.
webster_full: INHABITANT, n. A dweller; one who dwells or resides permanently in a place, or who has a fixed residence, as distinguished from an occasional lodger or visitor.
INHABIT, v.t. To live or dwell in; to occupy as a place of settled residence.
WOE, n. Grief; sorrow; misery; a heavy calamity.
2. A curse; a denunciation of calamity.
OVERCOME, v.t. To conquer; to vanquish; to subdue.
scriptures: Revelation 12:12

Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.
Revelation 8:13

And I beheld, and heard an angel flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice, Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth by reason of the other voices of the trumpet of the three angels, which are yet to sound!
Revelation 12:11
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Hebrews 12:28
Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
corruption_summary: Revelation's dwellers on the earth are mined for a timetable of coming events, and the book's own pastoral purpose is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation has been made into a chart. Dispensational systems, following Darby and popularised by the Scofield notes, assign the trumpets and the woes to a mapped sequence of a future seven years and read the inhabiters of the earth as a population left behind after a secret removal of the church — a scheme unknown to any Reformation confession and unknown to the church for eighteen centuries. Whatever a reader concludes about the millennium, and the Reformed churches have held more than one view, this apparatus is a nineteenth-century novelty and it changes what the book is for. John wrote to seven real congregations under pressure, to tell them who wins.

The opposite error empties the woes altogether, treating them as symbols of the general human condition with no reference to any real judgment on any real people. Revelation 12:12 resists both. Its woe is genuine, its comfort is genuine, and both are addressed to the present: the devil's wrath is great because his time is short, which is precisely why the saints in verse 11 overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony rather than by escaping the conflict. The book was given to make suffering churches steadfast, not to make comfortable ones curious.
roots_summary: Greek katoikeo (G2730), to dwell or settle — the participle rendered inhabiters at Revelation 8:13, 12:12 and them that dwell upon the earth throughout the book.
roots_lines: Greek katoikeo (G2730) — to dwell, to settle permanently; its participle is the inhabiters of Revelation 8:13 and 12:12.
Greek ouai (G3759) — woe; sounded three times by the flying angel of Revelation 8:13.
Greek nikao (G3528) — to overcome, conquer; Revelation 12:11, and the promise attached to each of the seven letters.
Greek thumos (G2372) — hot anger, wrath; Revelation 12:12, of the devil who knows his time is short.
Revelation 13:8 identifies the class: they that dwell upon the earth, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb.
usage: “Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea!” — a class, not merely a population.
“Great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time” — the rage of a defeated enemy.
“They overcame him by the blood of the Lamb” — how the church answers the woe.
